warmup.q: Inside payer { } of a payment-request DSL with no @DslMarker, someone writes payee { name = "oops" } by mistake. What happens?
options: It doesn't compile: payee isn't a member of PartyBuilder
It compiles and calls payee on the outer PaymentRequestBuilder
It compiles and builds a payee nested inside the payer
It compiles and is ignored at run time
warmup.why: Both receivers are in scope inside payer { }, and Kotlin resolves an unqualified call against each of them, nearest first. PartyBuilder has no payee, so the outer builder's payee is used. @DslMarker exists to turn that into a compile error. The first option is what most people expect, which is exactly why the bug survives review.

sections.h: A lambda with receiver is a function whose first parameter is this
sections.html:
A Java builder call repeats the builder's name on every line: b.debit(...), b.credit(...), b.memo(...). Kotlin DSLs drop that prefix, and the whole trick is one type. First a word: the receiver of a call is the object it's called on. In sb.append(x), sb is the receiver. Inside a class's own methods the receiver is this, and you can leave it out.

A function type with a receiver, written A.() -> B, is a lambda that runs with an A as this. So inside its braces you call the A's members with no prefix, as if you were writing a method of A. apply, with and run in the standard library are built on it.

Java
// Java has no receiver lambdas. Its idiom: a Consumer that receives the builder as a parameter.
static String receipt(Consumer<StringBuilder> block) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    block.accept(sb);
    return sb.toString();
}

receipt(sb -> sb.append("captured ").append(1_999));
Kotlin
fun receipt(block: StringBuilder.() -> Unit): String = StringBuilder().apply(block).toString()

receipt { append("captured "); append(1_999) }    // `this` is the StringBuilder

To the JVM, StringBuilder.() -> Unit and (StringBuilder) -> Unit are the same thing: a kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<StringBuilder, Unit>. The receiver is just the first argument. That's why Kotlin lets you assign one type to the other, and why you can call a receiver lambda both ways, sb.withReceiver() or withReceiver(sb). The difference exists only in the compiler, which decides what this means inside the braces.

It is also exactly what Java sees. Java calls receipt with a Function1, gets the builder as a parameter, and must end with return Unit.INSTANCE, because a Kotlin () -> Unit returns a real Unit object.

Two more facts make DSLs work. A receiver lambda can take parameters too: Builder.(Int) -> Unit gets a this and an Int. And an extension function is a named lambda with receiver. fun EntryBuilder.payout(merchant: String, grossMinor: Long, feeBps: Int) can be called inside any EntryBuilder.() -> Unit block, which is how you add vocabulary to a builder you don't own. The worked example does that.

try.title: Call a receiver lambda both ways
steps: In ReceiverDemo.kt, try the reverse assignment: val back: (StringBuilder) -> Unit = withReceiver. Predict whether it compiles, then run.
In the Java twin, delete return Unit.INSTANCE; from the first lambda and run. Read javac's complaint.

code.title: ReceiverDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo // Two function types. Inside the first, the StringBuilder is `this`; in the second it's a parameter. val withReceiver: StringBuilder.() -> Unit = { append("EUR "); append(19.99) } val withParameter: (StringBuilder) -> Unit = { sb -> sb.append("EUR ").append(19.99) } /** An ordinary function that takes a lambda with receiver: the smallest possible DSL entry point. */ fun receipt(block: StringBuilder.() -> Unit): String = StringBuilder().apply(block).toString() fun main() { val sb = StringBuilder() sb.withReceiver() // call it like an extension function... withReceiver(sb) // ...or pass the receiver as the first argument println(sb) val swapped: StringBuilder.() -> Unit = withParameter // the two types are interchangeable println(receipt(swapped)) println(receipt { append("captured "); append(1_999) }) println("JVM type of withReceiver: ${withReceiver.javaClass.interfaces.joinToString { it.name }}") }

alt.title: ReceiverDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo; import kotlin.Unit; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** * Java twin of ReceiverDemo.kt. Java has no lambdas with receivers. A Kotlin * StringBuilder.() -> Unit is a Function1<StringBuilder, Unit> to Java: the receiver is the first parameter. */ public class ReceiverDemoJava { // Java's own idiom for the same job: a Consumer that gets the builder as a parameter static String receiptJava(Consumer<StringBuilder> block) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); block.accept(sb); return sb.toString(); } public static void main(String[] args) { String r = ReceiverDemoKt.receipt(sb -> { sb.append("captured ").append(1_999); return Unit.INSTANCE; // Kotlin's Unit is a real object here }); System.out.println(r); System.out.println(receiptJava(sb -> sb.append("refunded ").append(500))); StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); ReceiverDemoKt.getWithReceiver().invoke(sb); // a receiver lambda, invoked with the receiver as argument System.out.println(sb); } }

try.expect: Kotlin prints EUR 19.99EUR 19.99 (one call as an extension, one with the receiver as an argument), EUR 19.99, captured 1999, and JVM type of withReceiver: kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1. The reverse assignment compiles too. Without return Unit.INSTANCE, javac stops with incompatible types: bad return type in lambda expression and missing return value: Function1.invoke returns an Object, so a Java lambda for it has to return something.

sections.h: A DSL is builder classes plus functions that take receiver lambdas
sections.html:
A type-safe builder has two pieces. A builder class holds the state and offers the vocabulary: properties to set and functions to call. An entry function creates the builder, runs your lambda on it and returns the result: Builder().apply(block).build(). Nesting is the same trick again: a builder function that takes another receiver lambda. Lesson 3 of the patterns track built a payment-request DSL this way, and the Kotlin docs build HTML from nothing more than classes, extension functions and function literals with receiver. You need no library.

The standard library ships three small builders you can use today:

Java
List<Item> building = new ArrayList<>();
building.add(new Item("sku-1", 2, 999));
building.add(new Item("sku-2", 1, 500));
if (building.size() == 2) building.add(new Item("gift-wrap", 1, 0));
List<Item> items = List.copyOf(building);            // freeze it with a copy

String text = new StringBuilder().append("total=").append(2_498).toString();
Kotlin
val items = buildList {
    add(Item("sku-1", 2, 999))
    add(Item("sku-2", 1, 500))
    if (size == 2) add(Item("gift-wrap", 1, 0))   // `this` is a MutableList
}
val totals = buildMap { for (i in items) put(i.sku, i.qty * i.unitMinor) }
val text = buildString { append("total="); append(totals.values.sum()) }

Inside buildList { }, this is a MutableList, so add, addAll and even size work. The result is typed List, and the demo shows it really is read-only: cast it back to MutableList, call add, and you get UnsupportedOperationException. That's what you want from a builder: mutable while you build, fixed once you're done. Java gets the same with List.copyOf, one copy later.

buildList, buildMap and buildString are inline, so their lambdas cost nothing (lesson 1 of this track). Your own entry functions can be inline too. Most DSL entry points run a few times per request, so it rarely matters.

Where does validation go? Check a single bad value at the call that passes it, so the error points at the wrong line: a debit of -100 fails inside debit. Check rules that span fields in build(), the one place that sees all of them: debits must equal credits. The lab does both.

try.title: Use the standard builders
steps: Run BuildersDemo and BuildersDemoJava. They print the same four lines.
In buildList { }, add println(this::class.simpleName) as the first line. Predict whether you'll see ArrayList, then run.
Move the if (size == 2) line above the two add calls and run again. What changed, and why?

code.title: BuildersDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo data class Item(val sku: String, val qty: Int, val unitMinor: Long) fun main() { val items = buildList { add(Item("sku-1", 2, 999)) add(Item("sku-2", 1, 500)) if (size == 2) add(Item("gift-wrap", 1, 0)) // `this` is a MutableList, so size works here } val totals = buildMap { for (i in items) put(i.sku, i.qty * i.unitMinor) } val text = buildString { append("total=") append(totals.values.sum()) } println(items.map { it.sku }) println(totals) println(text) try { @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") (items as MutableList<Item>).add(Item("late", 1, 1)) } catch (e: UnsupportedOperationException) { println("the built list is read-only: ${e.javaClass.simpleName}") } }

alt.title: BuildersDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * Java twin of BuildersDemo.kt. Java builds a mutable collection, then copies it into an * unmodifiable one. buildList and buildString are inline-only Kotlin functions, so Java can't call them. */ public class BuildersDemoJava { record ItemJava(String sku, int qty, long unitMinor) {} public static void main(String[] args) { List<ItemJava> building = new ArrayList<>(); building.add(new ItemJava("sku-1", 2, 999)); building.add(new ItemJava("sku-2", 1, 500)); if (building.size() == 2) building.add(new ItemJava("gift-wrap", 1, 0)); List<ItemJava> items = List.copyOf(building); Map<String, Long> totals = new LinkedHashMap<>(); for (ItemJava i : items) totals.put(i.sku(), i.qty() * i.unitMinor()); String text = new StringBuilder() .append("total=") .append(totals.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum()) .toString(); System.out.println(items.stream().map(ItemJava::sku).toList()); System.out.println(totals); System.out.println(text); try { items.add(new ItemJava("late", 1, 1)); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("the copied list is read-only: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); } } }

try.expect: Both print [sku-1, sku-2, gift-wrap], {sku-1=1998, sku-2=500, gift-wrap=0}, total=2498 and a line saying the list is read-only. Inside the block, this is the standard library's own list builder class (it prints ListBuilder), not an ArrayList: that's how the result can become read-only without a copy. With the if first, size is 0, so no gift-wrap line is added.

sections.h: @DslMarker makes only the nearest receiver implicit
sections.html:
Nesting creates a trap. Inside payer { } two receivers are in scope: the PartyBuilder and the outer PaymentRequestBuilder. Kotlin resolves an unqualified call against all of them, nearest first. So payee { } written inside payer { } compiles, because it finds payee on the outer builder. In the demo, without a marker, that misplaced line builds a second party and the program fails at run time with IllegalArgumentException: iban required for 'oops'. In a DSL without a required field, it would simply build the wrong request.

@DslMarker closes the hole. Annotate an annotation class with it, then put that annotation on every builder class. From then on, inside a block only the nearest marked receiver is implicit:

Java
// Java needs no marker: each lambda names its builder, so reaching the outer one takes `r.`
DslMarkerDemoKt.paymentRequest("PR-1", r -> {
    r.payer(p -> {
        p.setName("ACME Ltd");
        r.setCurrency("EUR");          // deliberate, and visible in review
        return Unit.INSTANCE;
    });
    return Unit.INSTANCE;
});
Kotlin
@DslMarker
@Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS, AnnotationTarget.TYPE)
annotation class PaymentDsl

@PaymentDsl class PartyBuilder { /* ... */ }
@PaymentDsl class PaymentRequestBuilder(private val id: String) { /* ... */ }

paymentRequest("PR-2") {
    payer {
        name = "ACME Ltd"
        payee { name = "oops" }                 // error: cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver
        this@paymentRequest.currency = "EUR"    // an explicit label still works
    }
}

The full message is 'fun payee(block: PartyBuilder.() -> Unit): Unit' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Use an explicit receiver if necessary. The label this@paymentRequest uses the name of the function that took the lambda, and nobody types it by accident.

The rules are narrow, so learn them exactly. The docs say a marker counts only on classes, on the receiver types of function types (the TYPE target, as in @PaymentDsl PartyBuilder.() -> Unit) and on type aliases. On a function or a property it "has no effect". Marking a common superclass is enough, so a DSL with twenty builders can mark one base class. And extension functions on a marked builder still work inside its block, because they resolve against the nearest receiver.

try.title: Watch the marker catch a misplaced call
steps: Run DslMarkerDemo (or its Java twin). Both print the same PaymentRequest, with currency EUR.
Uncomment the wrong-move block at the end of main. Predict, then run.
Now remove @PaymentDsl from both builder classes (keep the annotation class) and run again.
Put the markers back, and move one @PaymentDsl onto the payer function instead of PartyBuilder. Does the error come back?

code.title: DslMarkerDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo @DslMarker @Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS, AnnotationTarget.TYPE) annotation class PaymentDsl data class Party(val name: String, val iban: String) data class PaymentRequest(val id: String, val currency: String, val payer: Party, val payee: Party) @PaymentDsl class PartyBuilder { var name = "" var iban = "" fun build(): Party { require(iban.isNotBlank()) { "iban required for '$name'" } return Party(name, iban) } } @PaymentDsl class PaymentRequestBuilder(private val id: String) { var currency = "EUR" private var payer: Party? = null private var payee: Party? = null fun payer(block: PartyBuilder.() -> Unit) { payer = PartyBuilder().apply(block).build() } fun payee(block: PartyBuilder.() -> Unit) { payee = PartyBuilder().apply(block).build() } fun build() = PaymentRequest(id, currency, checkNotNull(payer) { "payer missing" }, checkNotNull(payee) { "payee missing" }) } fun paymentRequest(id: String, block: PaymentRequestBuilder.() -> Unit): PaymentRequest = PaymentRequestBuilder(id).apply(block).build() fun main() { val req = paymentRequest("PR-1") { currency = "GBP" payer { name = "ACME Ltd"; iban = "GB33BUKB20201555555555" } payee { name = "Corner Shop" iban = "GB94BARC10201530093459" this@paymentRequest.currency = "EUR" // an outer receiver needs an explicit label } } println(req) // Wrong move. Uncomment the block, predict, run. Then remove @PaymentDsl from both builder // classes and run it again. // paymentRequest("PR-2") { // payer { // name = "ACME Ltd" // payee { name = "oops" } // iban = "GB33BUKB20201555555555" // } // } }

alt.title: DslMarkerDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo; import kotlin.Unit; /** * Java twin of DslMarkerDemo.kt. Java calls the same Kotlin DSL with Function1 lambdas. It needs no * marker: each block names its builder, so reaching the outer one means typing `r.` on purpose. */ public class DslMarkerDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { PaymentRequest req = DslMarkerDemoKt.paymentRequest("PR-1", r -> { r.setCurrency("GBP"); r.payer(p -> { p.setName("ACME Ltd"); p.setIban("GB33BUKB20201555555555"); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); r.payee(p -> { p.setName("Corner Shop"); p.setIban("GB94BARC10201530093459"); r.setCurrency("EUR"); // the outer builder, named explicitly return Unit.INSTANCE; }); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); System.out.println(req); } }

try.expect: With the markers, the build fails with 'fun payee(block: PartyBuilder.() -> Unit): Unit' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Without them it compiles, runs, and dies with IllegalArgumentException: iban required for 'oops', thrown while building the misplaced payee. With the marker on the function and not the class, the wrong move compiles again: a marker on a function has no effect, and PartyBuilder is no longer a marked receiver.

sections.h: Calling a DSL from Java, and what became of context receivers
sections.html:
A Kotlin DSL works from Java, though it isn't pretty. Every Builder.() -> Unit parameter is a Function1<Builder, Unit>, so the Java caller writes b -> { b.debit(...); return Unit.INSTANCE; }, and the lab's LedgerFromJavaTest does just that. If Java callers matter, add a thin overload that takes a java.util.function.Consumer and give it its own name, so Kotlin callers never have to choose between two lambda types:

Java
JournalEntry e = LedgerKt.journalEntryJava("payout-981", b -> {
    b.debit("merchant:981", 12_000L);
    b.credit("bank:clearing", 12_000L);      // a void lambda: no Unit.INSTANCE
});
Kotlin
fun journalEntryJava(id: String, block: Consumer<EntryBuilder>): JournalEntry =
    journalEntry(id) { block.accept(this) }   // `this` is the EntryBuilder

@DslMarker means nothing to Java. A Java lambda names its parameter, so the scope problem doesn't arise.

DSLs were also the main reason for an experiment you'll still find in older code and blog posts: context receivers. Kotlin 1.6.20 shipped them as a prototype behind -Xcontext-receivers, and its release notes warned that the compiler would "produce pre-release binaries that cannot be used in production code". They let a function demand a receiver from its surroundings, as in context(Logger) fun audit(), so a DSL function could require being called inside some scope. Kotlin 2.2.0 replaced them with context parameters, and the 2.3.20 notes say it plainly: "Experimental context receivers are no longer supported and are replaced by context parameters."

In Kotlin 2.4.21 the old syntax fails twice: context parameters must be named. Use '_' to declare an anonymous context parameter. and then unresolved reference 'log', because a context parameter is not a receiver in the body. The old flag fails too: experimental context receivers are superseded by context parameters. Remove the '-Xcontext-receivers' compiler argument and migrate to the new syntax. When you see either message, the fix is the next lesson: context parameters, stable since Kotlin 2.4.0.

A check before you move on: a Java caller passes b -> { b.debit("merchant:981", 100L); b.credit("bank:clearing", 100L); } to journalEntry, with no return at the end. Predict what javac says, and why the same lambda is fine for journalEntryJava. (The answer follows from the two interfaces: Function1.invoke returns a value, and Consumer.accept returns void.)

analogy: A lambda with receiver is like being handed a form already clipped to a clipboard: inside the block you write on that form without saying which one. Nested blocks stack forms on top of each other, and without @DslMarker a field that doesn't exist on the top form gets written onto the form underneath, without anyone noticing. The marker says only the top form may be written on without naming it. The analogy breaks in a good way: a clerk finds the misfiled field after the forms are sent, while the compiler finds it before the code ever runs.
world: Payment services build nested data all day: a payout batch with entries and postings, routing rules per merchant, a test fixture for a Kafka event with its headers. A small DSL makes Quarkus tests and fixtures read like the data they produce, and it puts the validation (debits equal credits, every party has an IBAN) in one build() instead of in every test. Keep DSLs for nested data that many people write; a flat request with six fields is clearer with named arguments. Put @DslMarker in from the first day. Adding it later breaks every call site that was quietly reaching an outer builder, which is the point, but finding them in a hundred tests is a bad afternoon.
mistake:
Putting the marker on the builder functions instead of the builder classes, or leaving one builder unmarked. @PaymentDsl fun payer(...) compiles and does nothing: the docs say a marker on a function or property has no effect. The scope check starts only when the receiver types themselves (the builder classes, or one common superclass) carry the annotation:

Java
// Java has no equivalent rule to get wrong: the outer builder is always reached by name
r.payer(p -> { p.setName("ACME Ltd"); return Unit.INSTANCE; });
Kotlin
@PaymentDsl fun payer(block: PartyBuilder.() -> Unit) { ... }   // no effect at all

@PaymentDsl class PartyBuilder { ... }                         // this is what the check needs

Test your DSL by writing a misplaced call on purpose. If payee { } inside payer { } compiles, your marker isn't doing anything.

compare.title: A journal-entry builder: Java Consumer vs Kotlin lambda with receiver

java.title: Journal.java
java.html: public final class Journal { public static JournalEntry entry(String id, Consumer<EntryBuilder> block) { EntryBuilder b = new EntryBuilder(id); block.accept(b); // the builder arrives as a parameter return b.build(); } } JournalEntry e = Journal.entry("payout-981", b -> { b.memo("merchant payout"); b.debit("merchant:981", 12_000); b.credit("bank:clearing", 11_850); b.credit("revenue:fees", 150); });

kotlin.title: Journal.kt
kotlin.html: fun journalEntry(id: String, block: EntryBuilder.() -> Unit): JournalEntry = EntryBuilder(id).apply(block).build() // the builder is `this` inside block val e = journalEntry("payout-981") { memo = "merchant payout" debit("merchant:981", 12_000) credit("bank:clearing", 11_850) credit("revenue:fees", 150) }

compare.note: Both compile to the same thing: a function object that receives the builder. On the JVM, Kotlin's EntryBuilder.() -> Unit is a Function1<EntryBuilder, Unit>, and Java's Consumer<EntryBuilder> plays the same role. The difference is only in the source: Kotlin makes the builder this, so the block reads like a list of statements, and nested blocks need @DslMarker to stop calls from reaching outer builders by accident. Java names the parameter every time, which is noisier but can never resolve a call against the wrong builder.

worked.title: Add vocabulary to the ledger DSL with an extension function

steps.say: Every merchant payout is the same three postings: debit the merchant's balance, credit the bank with the net amount, credit fee revenue. Written out each time, the arithmetic gets copied, and one day it's copied wrong.
steps.code: Journal.entry("payout-981", b -> { b.debit("merchant:981", 12_000); b.credit("bank:clearing", 12_000 - 150); b.credit("revenue:fees", 150); });

alt.html: journalEntry("payout-981") { debit("merchant:981", 12_000) credit("bank:clearing", 12_000 - 150) credit("revenue:fees", 150) }

steps.say: Write an extension function on the builder. It works even if EntryBuilder lives in a library you can't edit, and inside a block it reads like a built-in word.
steps.code: // 1. compute the fee once, in one place fun EntryBuilder.payout(merchant: String, grossMinor: Long, feeBps: Int) { val fee = grossMinor * feeBps / 10_000 // 2. the three postings, always balanced debit("merchant:$merchant", grossMinor) credit("bank:clearing", grossMinor - fee) credit("revenue:fees", fee) } journalEntry("payout-981") { payout("981", 12_000, feeBps = 125) }

alt.html: // Java's version is a static helper that takes the builder as its first parameter, // which is exactly what the Kotlin extension compiles to static void payout(EntryBuilder b, String merchant, long grossMinor, int feeBps) { long fee = grossMinor * feeBps / 10_000; b.debit("merchant:" + merchant, grossMinor); b.credit("bank:clearing", grossMinor - fee); b.credit("revenue:fees", fee); }

steps.say: Check where it can be called. Inside entry { } it resolves against the nearest receiver, the EntryBuilder. Inside batch { } but outside an entry, it doesn't compile, so a payout can't be posted outside an entry by accident.
steps.code: batch("batch-17") { entry("payout-982") { payout("982", 8_000, 125) } // fine payout("983", 5_000, 125) // error: candidate 'fun EntryBuilder.payout(...): Unit' is inapplicable because of a receiver type mismatch. }

alt.html: Batches.batch("batch-17", bb -> { bb.entry("payout-982", b -> payout(b, "982", 8_000, 125)); // fine // payout(bb, "983", 5_000, 125); // error: incompatible types: BatchBuilder cannot be converted to EntryBuilder });

steps.say: Run it: the entry has postings of 12,000 debit, 11,850 and 150 credit, and build() accepts it because the debits equal the credits. Integer division rounds the fee down, so the bank gets the extra cent. Whether that's right is a business rule, and it's now in one function you can test.

steps: Run the tests. All seven fail.

drill.title: Write a tiny CSV-line DSL from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write csvLine { field("pay_7"); field(1_999); field("EUR") } returning "pay_7,1999,EUR": a builder class with field(value: Any) and an entry function that takes a lambda with receiver. Then write the Java version with a Consumer. Which line in the Kotlin version makes the builder this?

answer.html: class CsvLine { private val fields = mutableListOf<String>() fun field(value: Any) { fields += value.toString() } fun build(): String = fields.joinToString(",") } // the parameter type CsvLine.() -> Unit is what makes the builder `this` inside the braces fun csvLine(block: CsvLine.() -> Unit): String = CsvLine().apply(block).build() val line = csvLine { field("pay_7"); field(1_999); field("EUR") } // pay_7,1999,EUR

alt.title: CsvLine.java
alt.html: final class CsvLine { private final List<String> fields = new ArrayList<>(); void field(Object value) { fields.add(String.valueOf(value)); } String build() { return String.join(",", fields); } static String csvLine(Consumer<CsvLine> block) { CsvLine b = new CsvLine(); block.accept(b); // the builder is a parameter, not `this` return b.build(); } } String line = CsvLine.csvLine(b -> { b.field("pay_7"); b.field(1_999); b.field("EUR"); });

recap: A.() -> B is a function type with receiver: inside the lambda, the A is this. On the JVM it's a Function1<A, B>, interchangeable with (A) -> B.
A DSL is builder classes plus entry functions of the form Builder().apply(block).build(). No library is needed.
buildList, buildMap and buildString give you a mutable receiver while building and a read-only result.
Validate single values at the call, and cross-field rules in build().
@DslMarker on the builder classes makes only the nearest receiver implicit; reach outer ones with this@label. On functions it does nothing.
Java calls a DSL with Function1 lambdas that return Unit.INSTANCE. Context receivers are gone since 2.3.20; context parameters replace them.

explain.prompt: A teammate's test builds a payment request with payee { } accidentally written inside payer { }, and it compiled. Explain why it compiled, and what @DslMarker changes.
explain.answer: Inside payer { } there are two implicit receivers: the PartyBuilder the block was given, and the outer PaymentRequestBuilder from the paymentRequest { } block around it. When Kotlin sees an unqualified call, it tries each receiver in scope, nearest first. PartyBuilder has no payee, so the compiler found payee on the outer builder and called that, which built a second party in the wrong place. Nothing in the types was wrong, so it compiled. @DslMarker is a rule about those receivers: if the builder classes carry the same marker annotation, only the nearest marked receiver is implicit inside a block. The misplaced payee { } becomes a compile error that says it can't be called with an implicit receiver. If you really mean the outer builder, you name it with this@paymentRequest, which nobody writes by accident. The marker has to be on the builder classes; putting it on the functions does nothing.

deeper.html:
Context parameters, the subject of the next lesson, interact with implicit receivers, and Kotlin 2.4.21 is strict about it. The KEEP for context parameters uses this example:

Java
// No Java twin: Java has neither receivers nor context parameters.
// The nearest idea is two parameters of the same type, where you must pick one by name.
static void moo(Cow cow) { System.out.println("moo from " + cow.name()); }
Kotlin
class Cow(val name: String) { fun moo() = println("moo from $name") }

with(Cow("receiver")) {
    context(Cow("context")) {
        moo()   // which Cow?
    }
}

The with block makes one Cow an implicit receiver, and the context(...) block brings a second Cow into scope as a context argument. A bare moo() would resolve against the receiver, which is probably not what the author meant. Kotlin 2.4.21 reports an error: call to 'fun moo(): Unit' defined in 'Cow' uses an implicit receiver shadowed by a context parameter. Make the receiver explicit using 'this' or 'contextOf<Cow>()'. The type-safe builders page calls this a warning. The compiler you run is what counts, and here it is stricter than the page.

A second detail: the TYPE target on the marker lets you mark one block without marking the class, as in fun payer(block: @PaymentDsl PartyBuilder.() -> Unit). That helps when the builder comes from a library you can't annotate. And when you design a DSL for others, keep each builder's surface small. Every public member is offered by the IDE inside the block, and every one of them is a word someone will eventually use in the wrong place.
